Simulate Prior Predictive Responses and Landscape Scales

Source: R/bayes_scale_prior_predictive.R
simulate_bayes_prior.Rd

Check what the complete set of priors implies before you fit. Each simulated data set draws every parameter from its prior and then generates responses for the prepared observations, including the scatter of individual observations around their means.

Usage

simulate_bayes_prior(object, nsim = 100L, seed = NULL)

Arguments

object

A multiScale_bayes() object. An object from method = "prepare" is enough. For a fitted object, the posterior draws are ignored and its specification supplies the same prior model.

nsim

Positive integer number of prior predictive data sets; default 100. More data sets explore the priors more thoroughly and use more memory.

seed

Optional positive integer simulation seed. Your own random-number state is restored afterward, even when simulation fails.

Value

A list with these elements.

  • responses: a data frame with one row per prepared observation and one column per simulated data set, named sim_1, sim_2, and so on. Values are counts for Poisson and NB2 models, success counts out of the prepared trial totals for binomial models, and response units for Gaussian models.

  • means: a data frame of the matching expected responses. Binomial values are success probabilities, so multiply by the trial totals for expected counts. Other families use the response scale. Each mean is conditional on its own prior draw and excludes observation noise. It is not an expectation over the whole prior.

  • log_scales: a named list with one matrix per landscape predictor. Rows are its distinct combinations of scale covariates and groups, labeled as in posterior_scales(), and columns match the simulated data sets. Entries are natural log distances in projected map units, so exponentiate medians and interval limits to read them as distances.

  • observation_ids: the prepared landscape ID of each observation, in the row order of responses and means.

  • priors: the complete prior settings used, with defaults filled in.

Read the simulations

Compare the simulated magnitudes, fractions of zeros, and scale quantiles with ranges that are scientifically plausible for your design. Extreme simulations show that a prior is loose for your design and may call for a tighter setting, such as a smaller beta_sd. They are not evidence of a poor posterior fit, and they do not choose a prior for you. vignette("v13-bayesian-scales", package = "multiScaleR") works through this check.

Broad distance priors can have infinite arithmetic moments, so summarize scales with log-scale summaries and distance quantiles. Broad response group-SD priors with a log link can also give infinite prior predictive count moments. A finite simulation does not show that a mean over prior replicates exists.

How the simulation works

Each data set uses one complete, independent prior parameter vector. All observations in a group share that vector's group effect, which keeps the dependence that the scale and response formulas specify. Scale effects and response effects are drawn separately, as the model specifies.

Simulation conditions on the prepared maps, fixed covariates, offsets, group identities, binomial trial totals, and the frozen predictor standardization. It uses no observed responses and no posterior draws, and it creates no new sites or years. No optional Bayesian package is needed. A nonfinite value stops with an error that names the replicate. Values are never clipped and draws are never replaced.

See also

multiScale_bayes(), simulate.multiScaleR_bayes(), posterior_scales(); vignette("v13-bayesian-scales", package = "multiScaleR").

Examples

example <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "bayesian-annual-example.rds",
  package = "multiScaleR"))
prepared <- multiScale_bayes(count ~ habitat + factor(year) + (1 | site),
  example$inputs, example$data, scales = list(habitat = ~1 + (1 | year)),
  row_id = "site_year", priors = list(scale_median = 250), method = "prepare")
prior <- simulate_bayes_prior(prepared, nsim = 20, seed = 63)

# Fraction of zero counts in each prior data set, against the observed 0.04
range(vapply(prior$responses, function(y) mean(y == 0), numeric(1)))
#> [1] 0.38 0.96
# The default priors are loose and allow far more zeros than were observed.

# Prior range of sigma for each year, in meters
exp(apply(prior$log_scales$habitat, 1, stats::quantile, c(.025, .5, .975)))
#>        year=2021 year=2022 year=2023  year=2024  year=2025
#> 2.5%    25.29771  29.68201  41.06089   20.14086   16.99735
#> 50%    153.85049 124.09453 236.44030  142.68248  208.76500
#> 97.5% 1240.57462 636.67590 678.33440 1929.74700 1334.93399
# These are prior scale intervals, not posterior estimates or evidence of fit.
